title: CR-18 / Module 2 / N2c — Internal Network Enumeration
description: Sweep a flat internal network from scratch and fingerprint every exposed service across seven undocumented hosts, finishing with a purely enumeration-based flag. Concludes with a short knowledge-check assessment.
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with TCP/IP networking (subnets, ports, common services)
No prior nmap experience required — covered in the background level
outcomes: Perform host discovery and service enumeration across an internal subnet with no prior documentation
Identify running services and versions using nmap script scanning
Recognise common service-level misconfigurations (anonymous FTP, anonymous SMB, exposed metrics)
Enumerate SMB shares without needing to exploit or retrieve anything from them
Build an accurate asset inventory purely from active scanning

levels.title: Introduction level
levels.content:
Welcome to the Internal Network Scanning & Enumeration lab.

The client has asked for an internal asset assessment. Their IT team admits they don't have a reliable, up-to-date inventory of what's actually running on their internal network — no host list, no service map, nothing you can trust. You're building that picture from nothing but your own scanning.

From your assessment machine, you'll identify your own position on the network, sweep for live hosts, fingerprint every service each one exposes, and infer each host's role purely from what you find. Along the way, one host will turn out to be more exposed than any reasonable inventory should ever allow — a file share reachable with no credentials at all. Naming that share is your proof that the enumeration is complete.

You have **30 minutes** for the scanning exercise. A short background level right after you get access covers every tool you'll need if you haven't used them before. A 10-minute knowledge-check follows once you're done — by then you'll already have everything you need to answer it from your own scan output.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
In the topology panel on the right, right-click **pentestvm** and select **Open Console**. Log in with username **user** and password **Password123**.


Once you're connected, submit the passkey **start-training** to unlock the next level.

levels.title: Background — scanning tools
levels.content:
No asset list is provided for this exercise — building one is the exercise. Everything below is tool syntax you may need; which tool applies to which host is for you to work out once you start scanning.

## Tools you'll use

**nmap** — the core scanning tool for this exercise.

    sudo nmap -sn <subnet>                # host discovery, no ports touched (sudo matters: an unprivileged sweep cannot use ARP and misses hosts)
    sudo nmap -sV -sC <target_ip>          # version detection + default scripts, the default deep scan
    sudo nmap -p <range> <target_ip>       # scan a specific port or range
    sudo nmap -sU -p <range> <target_ip>   # UDP scan (slower — narrow the port range first)
    sudo nmap -O <target_ip>               # OS fingerprinting
    nmap --script <script-name> <target_ip>  # run a specific NSE script, e.g. http-headers, ftp-anon

**curl** — fetch a URL and inspect the raw response, including headers you won't see in a browser easily.

    curl -I http://<target_ip>/            # headers only
    curl http://<target_ip>:<port>/        # full response body

**ftp** — connect to an FTP service; many misconfigured servers accept the username `anonymous` with any password or a blank one.

**smbclient** — enumerate Windows/Samba file shares. Listing a share does not require connecting to it or downloading anything.

    smbclient -L //<target_ip> -N          # list shares, -N = no password (null session)

**snmpwalk** — query an SNMP-enabled device for system information. Try the default community string `public` if none is documented.

    snmpwalk -v2c -c public <target_ip> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1

A full `nmap -sV -sC` against each host you discover will tell you almost everything you need to infer its role — a web server looks different from a mail server, which looks different from a database server, purely by the ports and banners it shows you.

levels.title: Build the Inventory
levels.content:
Start from nothing. Build the picture yourself.

Your objectives for this level:

* Identify your own address and the internal subnet you're on. Your workstation has more than one interface: one belongs to the platform's management network and is out of scope, the other is the network you are assessing. Work out which is which before you scan anything.
* Sweep the subnet and count how many hosts actually respond.
* Run a full service scan against every host you find and infer each one's likely role purely from the ports and banners it exposes — a web server, a mail server, a database, and so on.
* One host exposes a file share that can be listed with no credentials at all — no login, no password, nothing. Find it.

Submit the **name of that share** as your answer for this stage. You only need to list it — you do not need to connect to it or retrieve anything from it.

*Note: the knowledge-check after this level draws on what you observe across every host, not just the one with the exposed share — scan broadly, not just enough to find the flag.*
levels.solution:
* Find your subnet — `ip addr` → pentest VM 192.168.56.10 on 192.168.56.0/24.
* Sweep for hosts — `sudo nmap -sn 192.168.56.0/24` → seven target hosts respond, plus your own workstation and the gateway.
* Scan every host you find — `sudo nmap -sV -sC <ip>` for each address discovered. Two hosts show SMB (port 445) among their services.
* Check each for anonymous SMB access — `smbclient -L //<ip> -N` on each of the two. One refuses without credentials; the other lists a share called `Shared` with no authentication required at all.

**Answer: Shared**

hints.title: Know Where You Stand
hints.content:
Before scanning anything, confirm your own address and which subnet you're actually on. You will see more than one interface. One is the platform's own management network and is not part of the assessment — scanning it tells you nothing about the client. The lab network is the other one.

Useful command: `ip addr`.

hints.title: Count Before You Scan
hints.content:
Sweep the subnet for live hosts before running deep scans against individual addresses — it tells you how many targets you're really dealing with.

Useful command: `sudo nmap -sn <subnet>`. Run it with sudo — an unprivileged sweep cannot use ARP and will miss any host that does not answer on tcp/80 or tcp/443.

hints.title: Profile Every Host
hints.content:
Run a full version/script scan against every address you discovered. You don't have a role for any of them yet — the open ports and service banners are the only source of truth you have.

Useful command: `nmap -sV -sC <ip>` — repeat for every host from your sweep.

hints.title: A Share With No Lock
hints.content:
More than one host in this network runs SMB. Only one of them will let you list its shares with no credentials whatsoever. Try a null session against each.

Useful command: `smbclient -L //<target_ip> -N`.

levels.title: Knowledge Check

questions.text: Excluding your own workstation and the gateway, how many hosts did your sweep of 192.168.56.0/24 find?
What is the Common Name (CN) on the HTTPS certificate served by 192.168.56.58?
What is the newest TLS protocol version supported by 192.168.56.58?
What is the name of the Git repository exposed on 192.168.56.75's Git service (port 9418)?
192.168.56.75's FTP service allows anonymous login. What flag did you retrieve from README.txt on that share?
What mail transfer agent software is running on the host at 192.168.56.127?
192.168.56.186 exposes a metrics endpoint on port 9100 with no authentication. What secret value did it leak?
How many SSH encryption algorithms are supported by the host running PostgreSQL (192.168.56.152)?
Per nmap's OS fingerprinting, what is 192.168.56.201 most likely running?
192.168.56.201 exposes an RDP service. What target/computer name does it report?

levels.instructions: Answer using what you already found while scanning in the previous level — no new scanning is required. Ten questions cover findings from across every host you enumerated, not just the one with the exposed share. Hosts are referenced by IP, the same way you found them. You have 10 minutes.

levels.title: Lab Completed
levels.content: You've completed the Internal Network Scanning & Enumeration lab. Starting from nothing but a subnet, you built a full picture of seven hosts and found a file share that should never have been reachable without credentials — a straightforward listing command, not an exploit. This kind of gap is one of the most common and most valuable findings in an internal engagement, and it never requires more than careful, thorough enumeration to surface. Head back to the LMS to continue the course.
